content: In the pharmaceutical industry, encapsulation refers to a variety of techniques used to enclose medications within a stable shell, known as a capsule. This allows the medication to be administered orally or used as suppositories. Capsules are primarily classified into two types: hard-shelled capsules, which are typically used for dry, powdered ingredients, and soft-shelled capsules, which are mainly used for oils or active ingredients dissolved or suspended in oil. Both types of capsules can be made from gelatin or plant-based gelling agents, such as carrageenans, modified starch, or cellulose. Since their introduction, capsules have been regarded by consumers as one of the most efficient methods of taking medication. This perception has led drug manufacturers, particularly those producing over-the-counter analgesics, to develop caplets (capsule-shaped tablets) to associate the positive attributes of capsules with the more cost-effective production of tablets. However, following the 1982 Tylenol tampering incidents, capsules experienced a slight decline in popularity as tablets were perceived to be more resistant to tampering. Soft Gel Encapsulation In 1834, Mothes and Dublanc were granted a patent for a method to produce single-piece gelatin capsules sealed with a drop of gelatin solution. Their process involved the use of individual iron molds, with the capsules being filled manually using a medicine dropper. Later, methods were developed that utilized sets of plates with pockets to form the capsules. While some companies still use this plate-based method, the equipment is no longer commercially produced. In 1933, P. Scherer introduced a significant innovation by using a rotary die process to manufacture capsules. This method involved blow molding to fill the capsules, which reduced material waste and was the first process to produce capsules with highly consistent dosages. In 1949, the Lederle Laboratories division of the American Cyanamid Company developed the Accogel process, which allowed powders to be accurately filled into soft gelatin capsules. Two-Part Gelatin Capsules In 1847, James Murdock patented the two-part telescoping gelatin capsule in London. These capsules are manufactured in two separate parts by dipping metal rods into molten gelatin solution. The capsules are supplied as closed units to pharmaceutical manufacturers. Before use, the two halves are separated, and the capsule is filled with powder. This can be done either by inserting a compressed slug of powder into one half of the capsule or by filling one half with loose powder. The other half of the capsule is then pressed on to close it. The advantage of using a compressed slug of powder is that it provides better control over weight variation. However, the machinery required for this process is more complex compared to filling with loose powder.
